. A histogram summarizes one numerical
variable’s

gf_histogram(~ width, data = KidsFeet, bins = 10, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white",
             xlab = "Foot width (cm)", ylab = "Count",
             title = "Foot width of 39 kids")

a roughly mound-shaped histogram of the 39 widths, with a tall
bar near 8.9 cm, a smaller dip around 9.1–9.3 cm, and bars tapering off toward the
low (7.9 cm) and high (9.8 cm) ends — consistent with the mean of about 9.0 and SD
of about 0.5 you already saw in

, a set of colors
chosen to stay distinguishable for colorblind readers — every figure in this course
uses it (or the closely related
palette) instead of R’s default colors.
A boxplot compares a numerical variable

in one compact picture —
put the grouping variable on the right of

gf_boxplot(width ~ sex, data = KidsFeet, fill = ~ sex) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00"))) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Sex (B = boy, G = girl)", y = "Foot width (cm)",
          title = "Foot width by sex")

two boxes side by side. The boys’ box sits noticeably higher
(median line near 9.15 cm) than the girls’ box (median line near 8.80 cm), matching
the group means from

above; both boxes have roughly similar height
(spread), and neither shows an extreme outlier point.

gf_bar(~ domhand, data = KidsFeet, fill = ~ domhand) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00"))) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Dominant hand", y = "Count", title = "Dominant hand of 39 kids")

two bars, “L” and “R.” The “R” bar is much taller (31 kids)
than the “L” bar (8 kids) — right-handed kids clearly outnumber left-handed kids
in this sample, which you can also confirm with

between two numerical variables —
one point per observation:

gf_point(width ~ length, data = KidsFeet, color = ~ sex, shape = ~ sex) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00"))) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Foot length (cm)", y = "Foot width (cm)",
          title = "Foot width vs. length, by sex")

a cloud of 39 points trending up and to the right — as foot
length increases, width tends to increase too (a positive association) — with
circles marking boys and triangles marking girls, colored differently as well.
Notice the shapes are

different, not just the colors — this course’s plots
never rely on color alone to separate groups, so the picture still reads clearly in
grayscale or for a colorblind viewer.
You can back up that “trending up” impression with a single descriptive number,

(the correlation coefficient — a bonus tool for this course, since MATH
1209 doesn’t test formal inference on relationships between two numerical
variables):

A correlation of about 0.64 is a moderately strong positive relationship — bigger
feet tend to be both longer

wider, which is exactly what the upward-trending
scatterplot showed you.
